source.title: Offline Q-Learning on Diverse Multi-Task Data Both Scales And Generalizes
source.authors: Aviral Kumar; Rishabh Agarwal; Xin-Yang Geng; G. Tucker; S. Levine

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses language-model scaling laws as motivation and analogy, but its own results measure Atari reinforcement-learning performance, not any of the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. and describes its own offline RL performance trends as analogous to scaling laws. It does not measure held-out language-model loss, fit or test language-model loss power laws, test extrapolation of those fits, or study compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Its Atari scaling results are recorded under fits_no_version; cited scaling results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study scales offline Q-learning on multi-task Atari and reports human-normalized game scores against model size. It never measures held-out pretraining loss, fits power laws, or tests extrapolation, compute allocation or architecture shape at fixed size. The intro's 'power-law relationship between model capacity and performance' is an RL-return trend with no fitted law. It is a related construct, not loss scaling, so it falls outside V5 and the other versions. Kaplan et al. is cited only as an analogy.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that, with ResNets, C51 distributional backups and feature normalization, offline Q-learning performance scales favorably with capacity. They describe this as akin to Kaplan-style scaling laws, but give no fitted law. They attribute the poor prior scaling to the IMPALA architecture. They also claim the method exceeds the performance in the dataset and that its representations transfer to new games.
record.recipe_differences: Offline conservative Q-learning on multi-task Atari, measuring task scores across RL model sizes; it does not use language-model loss scaling procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling trend changes with architecture family: ResNet performance rises with size, while IMPALA performance degrades. The paper also reports different absolute performance for MSE and C51 TD errors.

fits_no_version.finding: Offline multi-task Atari CQL returns rise with modified ResNet size (34/50/101/152) for both MSE and C51 TD error. C51 scores higher in absolute terms (Table 1: ResNet101 median 98.9% vs 59.5% with MSE). Returns fall with size for the IMPALA family, a result cited from Lee et al. Discrete-BCQ also improves from ResNet34 to ResNet50 (Fig. A.3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Offline RL return improves with model capacity, but only for some architecture families and TD-loss formulations.

record.problems: The main experiments use one seed, as the paper states. Figure 6 does not provide numerical values in the text, and the IMPALA scaling comparison is taken from Lee et al. (2022).

untested.parts: No language-model held-out loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No small-run fits used to predict larger runs.
No compute-budget allocation between parameters and data.
No comparison of shape at a fixed parameter count; it compares architecture families across sizes.
No loss power-law fit in the RL regime; only qualitative trends in return with model size.
No downstream performance predicted from language-model scale or loss.
No study of how exponents or fitting choices change the result.

record.verdict_notes: The main experiments use a single seed. The scaling evidence is figure-only, with no fitted exponents. The ablations (Tables 1, 2 and A.1–A.3, Fig. A.3) concern design choices and offline RL scaling, not any version of the claim.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test language-model held-out pretraining loss or its dependence on parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run language-model loss fits or predictions of larger-run loss are tested.
No compute-budget allocation between language-model parameters and tokens is tested.
The paper compares architecture families as model size changes, not architecture differences at fixed parameter count or their effects on loss.
The paper studies offline RL, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds for loss in another modality or training regime.
The reported Atari scores are not downstream-task performance predicted from language-model scale or pretraining loss.
The paper does not test how language-model exponents or compute-optimal allocations vary with fitting choices, or whether language-model loss curves bend.

relation.reason: The introduction explicitly compares the capacity trend to Kaplan-style scaling laws; the method does not use or test a quantitative scaling law.

tranche.reason: The experiments establish qualitative RL return improvements with capacity, without testing power-law form, loss extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, fixed-size architecture invariance, or downstream scaling predictability. The introduction asserts a power-law relationship but supplies no fitted law or functional-form test.

source_check.notes: Main experiments use one seed. Section 5.1 states a 1M–100M architecture range, while Figure 6 displays parameter-axis ticks from 30M to 200M; neither supplies numerical curve endpoints.
